repos.name: ayghri / i-have-adhd
repos.description: A skill to stop your coding agent from burying the answer. ADHD-friendly output.

summary.goal: i-have-adhd is a skill/plugin for coding assistants such as Claude Code, designed to make responses action-first: leading with the next step, numbering multi-step tasks, and cutting filler such as 'Hope this helps!' instead of burying the actual answer in preamble.
summary.usage: Install by copying the prompt that references https://github.com/ayghri/i-have-adhd and the repo's AGENTS.md into a CLI, or follow INSTALL.md; within Claude Code the skill can also be installed with `claude plugin install i-have-adhd@i-have-adhd` and invoked with `/i-have-adhd`.
summary.pros: Behavior is governed by 10 explicit rules documented in SKILL.md, such as leading with the next action, numbering steps, and capping lists at 5 items, which likely produces predictable, terse output formatting.
summary.cons: Effective use appears to presume an environment that supports Claude Code-style skills/plugins, since installation and tuning rely on AGENTS.md and marketplace commands, so applicability outside that ecosystem or with other coding assistants is not fully detailed.
summary.fit: This seems best suited for developers using Claude Code who want concise, action-first assistant replies rather than conversational preamble; those preferring more explanatory responses may find the terse style less suitable.

repos.name: bilawalsidhu / gods-eye-view
repos.description: A spy satellite simulator in your browser, except the data is real. Live open source spatial intelligence on a photorealistic 3D globe.

summary.goal: God's Eye View is a browser-based 3D globe application that aggregates public live-data feeds—aircraft, ships, satellites, earthquakes, traffic, and public cameras—into a single explorable interface, with optional hands-free voice control via a realtime AI agent.
summary.usage: It can be installed with Pinokio (version 8.2 or later) for one-click setup, or run locally via `git clone https://github.com/bilawalsidhu/gods-eye-view.git`, `npm ci`, and `npm run dev`, then opened at `http://localhost:4173`. Node.js 24.x (24.14.0 or later) or 26.x is required. Optional API keys (Cesium ion, Google Maps, OpenAI) can be added afterward inside the app.
summary.pros: The app starts without any API keys, offering Esri satellite imagery and keyless terrain by default. Eleven of thirteen documented data layers—including flights, military traffic, satellites, earthquakes, and public cameras—work without signup. It's released under the MIT License, and configured keys are handled server-side.
summary.cons: Some data layers are approximations rather than direct observations: traffic is simulated along real roads from aggregate location data, and CCTV camera poses are coarse estimates requiring manual calibration. Voice features require a paid OpenAI key, and Node.js 25 is explicitly unsupported, flagged as end-of-life by the setup doctor.
summary.fit: The README describes this as an evolving open-source client 'for exploration and learning' rather than a hardened production service, suggesting it is best suited to developers, hobbyists, and researchers exploring geospatial data rather than safety-critical operational use. The documentation explicitly warns against relying on it for flight or maritime navigation, emergency response, or other safety-critical decisions, since underlying data may be delayed, incomplete, or wrong.

repos.name: nab138 / iloader
repos.description: User friendly sideloader

summary.goal: iloader is presented in the README as a desktop application for installing SideStore (or other apps) and importing pairing files. The README states that this repository and https://iloader.app are the only official download sources, while noting unofficial Homebrew, AUR, and Fedora COPR packages exist.
summary.usage: Per the README, setup involves installing usbmuxd (iTunes on Windows, included on macOS, package-manager install possibly needed on Linux), then downloading the latest release from https://github.com/nab138/iloader or using the NixOS flake. Users plug in an iDevice, open the app, sign into an Apple ID, and choose an action like installing SideStore. Building from source requires bun (or Node.js) and Rust, cloning the repo, running `bun i`, then `bun tauri dev` for development or `bun tauri build` for a production build.
summary.pros: According to the README, iloader can install SideStore (or LiveContainer plus SideStore) while automatically importing certificates and pairing files, import any IPA file, provide intelligent error suggestions, manage pairing files across apps such as StikDebug, Protokolle, and SideStore, and let users view and revoke development certificates and app IDs.
summary.cons: The README explicitly states that iloader 'needs localization,' which suggests some languages may still be missing or contain mistakes, implying non-English users could encounter incomplete translations until community contributions address them.
summary.fit: Given its emphasis on tools like SideStore, StikDebug, and Protokolle alongside credited libraries such as idevice and isideload, iloader appears best suited for users managing iOS sideloading and pairing files outside the App Store, rather than general-purpose app installation.

repos.name: melgarafael / DeskcommCRM
repos.description: Open-source AI sales OS — self-hosted CRM with native AI agents + WhatsApp (WAHA). Open alternative to Kommo, Octadesk & Intercom for any business that sells by chat. MCP-ready, multi-tenant, LGPD.

summary.goal: DeskcommCRM is described as an open-source, self-hosted 'AI Sales Operating System' for WhatsApp, combining a CRM with AI agents that attend, qualify, and sell, positioned as an alternative to Kommo, Octadesk, and Intercom.
summary.usage: The README documents installing on a VPS with a single command — either a guided setup script or `git clone https://github.com/melgarafael/DeskcommCRM.git` followed by `bash hostgator-setup-kit/install.sh`. Setup requires a domain, a Supabase account, and an AI provider key; WhatsApp connects via QR code (WAHA) or Meta's official channel.
summary.pros: Documented features include AI agents with per-tenant RAG that operate the CRM, automatic follow-ups for stalled leads, multi-tenant row-level security isolation, configurable vocabulary per business niche, and a Next.js 16 frontend stack, all under MIT licensing with no paid tier or locked features.
summary.cons: Support is described as community-based and provided 'as-is' with no guaranteed SLA. Additionally, the Supabase free tier does not include automatic backups, so scheduling the backup script is documented as advisable.
summary.fit: This appears suited for businesses selling via WhatsApp (e-commerce, clinics, real estate, agencies) that want self-hosted control of their data on a VPS with Docker, with 4 GB RAM recommended for installation.

repos.name: vastsa / PI-Desktop
repos.description: Local-first AI coding agent desktop: Electron + Rust host core + pi Agent Harness + user-installable plugins

summary.goal: PI-Desktop is a desktop workspace for AI coding agents, unifying projects, sessions, files, reviews, models, permissions, and extensions in one local-first, model-agnostic application for macOS, Windows, and Linux (lines 5-11). As an Early Preview, its scope may still evolve (lines 49-50).
summary.usage: Users download PI-Desktop from GitHub Releases, connect a model provider via Settings → Model configuration, then open a local project (lines 280-287). For development, clone the repo and run `pnpm install` and `pnpm dev` after building the Rust host core (lines 463-473).
summary.pros: Conversations, settings, and API credentials stay local (JSONL/SQLite, OS keychain), with no PI-Desktop telemetry and no mandatory hosted relay (lines 263-272). It supports multiple providers—OpenAI, Anthropic, and local gateways like Ollama and LM Studio—plus extensibility through Skills, MCP servers, Subagents, and installable Plugins (lines 246-251, 196-198).
summary.cons: PI-Desktop is explicitly an Early Preview, meaning APIs, extension interfaces, and some desktop behaviors are still evolving (lines 49-50). Plugin processes are permission-gated but remain user-trusted code rather than a full sandbox, so only trusted plugins should be installed (lines 215-216).
summary.fit: It appears best suited for developers wanting a persistent, cross-platform workspace for long-running agent sessions rather than disposable chats (lines 168-170). Stated priorities like macOS release qualification and stronger plugin sandboxing suggest some areas are still maturing (lines 434-440).

repos.name: armory3d / armorpaint
repos.description: Graphics Creation Tools

summary.goal: ArmorPaint is described as software for 3D PBR texture painting, with a manual available at https://armorpaint.org/manual. This repository contains the source code, aimed at developers, used to build the ArmorPaint application from source.
summary.usage: To build from source, clone the repository with `git clone https://github.com/armory3d/armorpaint` and move into the `armorpaint/paint` directory. Platform-specific build scripts are then run, for example `../base/make --run` on Linux, with similar make commands documented for Windows, macOS, Android, iOS, and WASM targets.
summary.pros: The README documents build support across multiple platforms, including Windows (x64), Linux (x64), macOS (arm64), Android (arm64), iOS (arm64), and WASM, plus tooling for generating locale files.
summary.cons: Building the git version requires a platform-specific compiler (e.g., Visual Studio with clang tools, Xcode, or Android Studio) and git installed beforehand; embedding data files further requires a compiler with c23 #embed support such as clang 19 or newer, and the repository notes it may not be stable.
summary.fit: This repository appears best suited to developers who want to compile ArmorPaint themselves or contribute to development, rather than end users seeking a ready-to-use application, since precompiled binaries are distributed separately and paid to help fund the project.

repos.name: alsk1992 / CloddsBot

summary.usage: Installation is done via `npm install -g https://github.com/alsk1992/CloddsBot/releases/latest/download/clodds.tgz --loglevel=error` followed by `clodds onboard`, which runs a setup wizard for API keys and messaging channels and starts a gateway; a built-in WebChat interface then opens at `http://localhost:18789/webchat`. repos.name: nashsu / llm_wiki
repos.description: LLM Wiki is a cross-platform desktop application that turns your documents into an organized, interlinked knowledge base — automatically. Instead of traditional RAG (retrieve-and-answer from scratch every time), the LLM incrementally builds and maintains a persistent wiki from your sources。

summary.goal: LLM Wiki is a cross-platform desktop application that turns imported documents into an organized, interlinked personal knowledge base, using an LLM to incrementally build and maintain a wiki rather than re-deriving answers on each query. It extends a documented pattern originally described by Andrej Karpathy, adding a full desktop implementation with knowledge graph, search, and review features.
summary.usage: To build from source, install Node.js 20+, Rust 1.88+, and protoc, then run `git clone https://github.com/nashsu/llm_wiki.git`, `npm install`, and `npm run tauri dev` for development or `npm run tauri build` for production. A local HTTP API runs at `http://127.0.0.1:19828`, and an agent skill can be added with `npx skills add https://github.com/nashsu/llm_wiki_skill.git --skill llm-wiki`.
summary.pros: Documented features include two-step chain-of-thought document ingest with source traceability, multimodal PDF image extraction with captions, multi-format parsing (PDF, Office, EPUB/MOBI), a 4-signal knowledge graph with Louvain community detection, optional vector semantic search via LanceDB, Deep Research web search integration, and a bundled MCP server for external AI agent access.
summary.cons: Vector semantic search is disabled by default and must be manually enabled with a separate embedding endpoint and API key in Settings, so out-of-the-box retrieval relies on tokenized keyword search and graph expansion alone. Building from source also requires Node.js 20+, Rust 1.88+, and protoc as prerequisites.
summary.fit: As a Tauri v2 desktop application distributed under the GNU General Public License v3.0, this tool appears best suited to individuals or teams building a personal or project-level knowledge base who want local-first storage and Obsidian-compatible wiki files, though the GPL-3.0 licensing terms may warrant review before use in proprietary commercial products.

repos.name: obra / superpowers
repos.description: An agentic skills framework & software development methodology that works.

summary.goal: Superpowers is described as a complete software development methodology for coding agents, built on composable skills paired with initial instructions that ensure the agent invokes them automatically.
summary.usage: Installation of Superpowers is harness-specific; for Claude Code, run `/plugin install superpowers@claude-plugins-official` from the official marketplace, or register a separate marketplace with `/plugin marketplace add obra/superpowers-marketplace` followed by `/plugin install superpowers@superpowers-marketplace`. Once installed, skills like brainstorming, writing-plans, and test-driven-development activate automatically to guide design, planning, and RED-GREEN-REFACTOR implementation.
summary.pros: The skills library covers testing, debugging, collaboration, and meta workflows, and the documented basic workflow emphasizes test-first development, code review between tasks, and evidence-based verification before completion. It supports multiple coding agents, including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Gemini CLI, among other supported harnesses.
summary.cons: Because installation differs by harness, using Superpowers with more than one coding agent requires installing it separately for each, which could add setup and update overhead.
summary.fit: This methodology appears best suited to teams already working with one of the supported coding agents who want a structured, mandatory design-to-implementation workflow, and may be less fitting for those seeking a lightweight, optional process.

repos.name: Sonarr / Sonarr
repos.description: Smart PVR for newsgroup and bittorrent users.

summary.usage: Sonarr is obtained via the Download/Installation page (https://sonarr.tv/#downloads-v3) and runs on major platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, and Raspberry Pi. It integrates with download clients SABnzbd and NZBGet and with media servers Kodi and Plex for library updates and notifications.

summary.cons: GitHub Issues are documented as limited to bug reports and feature requests only, so users seeking general help must rely on separate channels such as the Forums, Discord, IRC, or Reddit, which may add friction for casual questions.
summary.fit: Given its cross-platform support (Windows, Linux, macOS, Raspberry Pi) and integrations with SABnzbd, NZBGet, Kodi, and Plex, Sonarr appears best suited to users already running Usenet/BitTorrent download clients and home media servers who want automated episode management, and it is released under the GNU GPL v3 license (copyright 2010-2025).

repos.name: jihe520 / MathModelAgent
repos.description: 🤖📐专为数学建模设计的 Agent & skills ,自动完成数学建模，生成一份完整的可以直接提交的论文。 An Agent Designed for Mathematical Modeling ,Automatically complete mathmodel and generate a complete paper ready for submission.

summary.goal: MathModelAgent is a SKILL-driven automation tool built for mathematical modeling competitions. It analyzes a modeling problem, writes and debugs code, and produces a formatted paper intended to be submission-ready, running inside a Harness such as Claude Code or Codex. Its stated vision is to shorten a typical 3-day competition to about 1 hour, which reads as an aspirational goal rather than a guaranteed outcome.
summary.usage: Two setup paths are documented. A desktop app can be downloaded from https://github.com/jihe520/MathModelAgent/releases/latest and requires no separate Python, Node.js, or Redis install. Alternatively, developers can install the SKILL with `npx skills add jihe520/MathModelAgent --all`, then run it inside Claude Code via `claude --dangerously-skip-permissions` followed by the `/1start-mathmodel` command, or inside Codex via `codex --yolo`.
summary.pros: Listed capabilities include a multi-agent workflow with separate modeling, coding, and writing agents, support for any LLM via litellm, both local (Jupyter) and cloud (E2B, Daytona) code interpreters, 17 built-in Typst paper templates for major competitions, and a 9-step automated paper verification process.

summary.fit: The project appears best suited to individuals preparing for math modeling competitions such as MCM/ICM, with the desktop app aimed at non-technical users and the SKILL-based setup aimed at developers who want to self-host or customize behavior. The license permits personal, non-commercial use only, with commercial use requiring direct contact with the author.

repos.name: p1neappleXpress / OpenFlux
repos.description: Network stack research tool. TCP tunnel with pluggable transports.

summary.goal: OpenFlux is presented as a network stack research tool that implements a TCP tunnel with pluggable transports. Traffic flows from a SOCKS5 client through a selected transport to an exit node, which forwards packets to the internet.
summary.usage: Building the desktop client/exit-node binary requires `go mod tidy` followed by `go build -o universal-bypass-tool .`. The resulting `universal-bypass-tool` binary runs as a client via `./universal-bypass-tool --client --url "YOUR_YANDEX_DOC_URL" --socks5 :1080 --debug`, starting a local SOCKS5 proxy on port :1080; running it as an exit node instead requires root access on a Linux VPS/VDS host.
summary.pros: The project ships prebuilt clients: an Android APK at https://github.com/p1neappleXpress/OpenFluxAndroid and an iOS TestFlight beta at https://testflight.apple.com/join/BwnAcdus, alongside the Golang-based desktop/exit-node binary. Its Transport interface lets developers implement and register custom transports, and the two included transports (Yandex Docs cursor messages, MAX WebRTC DataChannel) offer different network-stack approaches.
summary.cons: Building the project requires specific toolchain versions — Golang 1.26.3+, Android NDK 27.0.12077973+, and XCode 26.6+ — which may limit use to environments with matching versions available. Running an exit node also requires root access and manual iptables configuration to suppress kernel-generated TCP RST packets, a workaround that can affect scanned-port behavior if applied host-wide instead of scoped to a dedicated IP.
summary.fit: OpenFlux is licensed under the GNU General Public License v3.0 or later and describes itself as educational and non-commercial, with no paid features. It appears best suited to users comfortable self-hosting a Linux exit node and configuring firewall rules, rather than as a turnkey consumer VPN, since the author disclaims responsibility for how OpenFlux is applied by others.

repos.name: jordan-gibbs / hyperresearch
repos.description: Agent-driven research knowledge base. Agents collect, search, and synthesize web research into a persistent, searchable wiki.

summary.goal: Hyperresearch is a tool that turns Claude Code into a deep-research agent, running a tier-adaptive 16-step pipeline from a single prompt to produce an adversarially-audited report with source citations, backed by a persistent, searchable vault. The README reports that it currently leads the DeepResearch-Bench RACE leaderboard, though this appears to be a self-reported, forward-looking projection rather than an independently confirmed result.
summary.usage: Install with `pip install hyperresearch && hyperresearch install` inside a project directory (Python 3.11–3.13 required), then invoke it in Claude Code with `/hyperresearch <anything>`.
summary.pros: Every citation is checked by a cite-checker before a report ships, adversarial critics review each draft, and sources are deduplicated across syndicated copies to avoid false consensus. Runs resume from a persisted manifest after a crash, and every fetched source is stored in a searchable markdown-plus-SQLite vault reused by later sessions.
summary.cons: The README describes the leaderboard comparison as a forward-looking projection from a stratified pilot with third-party validation still pending, so the benchmark standing is not yet independently verified. Python 3.14 is not yet supported, and usage cost scales with the chosen tier, gear, and corpus size since the agents run on Anthropic models.
summary.fit: This appears best suited to users already working inside Claude Code who need structured, source-verified research reports, since it requires Python 3.11+ and Claude Code itself to run. Its scaling from a roughly 30-minute bounded run up to multi-hour dissertation-length runs suggests it may fit both quick lookups and long-form research projects, though heavier tiers likely require more time and API usage.

repos.name: alphaXiv / OpenResearch
repos.description: Run parallel research agents with any model

summary.goal: OpenResearch is described as a local-first workspace for research agents and autoresearch, turning coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or Cursor into research agents that can review literature, develop hypotheses, run experiments, and produce research artifacts.
summary.usage: The CLI is installed with `curl -LsSf https://openresearch.sh/install.sh | sh` followed by `orx up`, which opens a local dashboard at `http://127.0.0.1:4791`; a desktop app is also downloadable from https://openresearch.sh/download, and remote GPU workspaces can be reached with `orx up --remote user@host`.
summary.pros: The README states OpenResearch provides parallel exploration through isolated git worktrees per agent session, reproducible experiments tracked in a git-native experiment tree with immutable commit archives, and local ownership of projects, logs, code, and artifacts, alongside a choice of agent and compute backend.

summary.fit: Given its ability to run the same committed source snapshot locally, over SSH, or on Slurm, Kubernetes, Ray, Hugging Face Jobs, Modal, Tinker, or managed OpenResearch compute without publishing the repository, it appears suited to teams wanting local-first control over research workflows with optional cloud-account features like organizations and managed compute.

repos.name: github / spec-kit
repos.description: 💫 Toolkit to help you get started with Spec-Driven Development

summary.goal: Spec Kit is presented as an open source toolkit for Spec-Driven Development, where specifications become executable and directly generate working implementations rather than just guiding them, for use with any AI coding agent.

Then run `specify init my-project --integration copilot` and `cd my-project`; inside the project, launch a coding agent and use workflow commands such as /speckit-constitution, /speckit-specify, /speckit-plan, /speckit-tasks, /speckit-implement, and /speckit-converge.

summary.fit: Given its focus on structured specifications, enterprise constraint handling, and role-based bundles, Spec Kit seems best suited to teams that want a repeatable, agent-assisted development process rather than ad hoc prompting, though actual fit likely depends on the AI coding agent and workflow already in use.

repos.name: pascalorg / editor
repos.description: Open-source 3D architectural editor with a local CLI, MCP tools, and practical workflows for humans and AI agents.

summary.goal: Pascal Editor is described as an open-source, local-first 3D building editor built with React Three Fiber and WebGPU. It can run in the browser or from a CLI, and supports connecting AI agents through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
summary.usage: Node.js 22.13 or newer is documented as enough to create a persistent local installation without cloning the repository, using `npx @pascal-app/cli editor`, which starts the editor and an authenticated MCP service in the background. The `pascal` command can also be installed globally with `npm install --global @pascal-app/cli`.
summary.pros: The repository is organized as a Turborepo monorepo with separate packages for core scene state/schemas, the viewer rendering runtime, editor UI tools, built-in node definitions, the CLI installer, and an MCP server, which suggests a modular, reusable architecture. Built-in MCP support also appears to let AI agents connect without extra custom tooling.

summary.fit: Given its MCP server package and CLI-based local installation path, Pascal Editor seems best suited to developers building or extending AI-agent-connected 3D scene or building-editing tools, with Node.js 22.13 or newer as a documented prerequisite.

repos.name: affaan-m / ECC
repos.description: The agent harness performance optimization system. Skills, instincts, memory, security, and research-first development for Claude Code, Codex, Opencode, Cursor and beyond.

summary.goal: ECC is an MIT-licensed open-source "agent harness operating system" that adds a structured engineering workflow (plan, test, implement, review, verify, remember, improve) on top of AI coding agents. It ships 68 agents, 292 skills, and 94 legacy command shims, plus hooks, rules, memory, and AgentShield security scanning, and works primarily with Claude Code.
summary.usage: The recommended install runs `npx ecc-universal@2.2.1 setup` for guided Claude Code plugin setup, or natively inside Claude Code via `/plugin marketplace add https://github.com/affaan-m/ECC` followed by `/plugin install ecc@ecc`. Only one install method should be used per harness to avoid duplicated skills, commands, or hooks.
summary.pros: ECC bundles a large, pre-built catalog (68 agents, 292 skills) covering planning, TDD, code review, build repair, security, and domain-specific workflows, so teams do not need to assemble this tooling from scratch. It also includes AgentShield scanning for prompts, hooks, MCP configs, and secrets, and supports self-hosted or custom model endpoints without changing ECC's workflows.
summary.cons: The README states ECC "works best with Claude Code today" and that adapters for other harnesses (Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini, Zed, Copilot, and others) are "capability-limited," so full feature parity across harnesses is not guaranteed and should be checked before assuming equivalent behavior. Setup also requires Node.js 18+, and Claude plugin setup additionally requires Git and Claude Code 2.1+.
summary.fit: ECC appears best suited for teams already standardized on Claude Code who want a structured, tool-assisted development workflow with reusable skills and security scanning. Teams relying primarily on other harnesses may get a reduced feature set, since the documented platform support table lists several integrations as beta, experimental, or instruction-only rather than at full parity.

repos.name: DietrichGebert / ponytail
repos.description: Makes your AI agent think like the laziest senior dev in the room. The best code is the code you never wrote.

summary.goal: Ponytail is a rule-set/plugin for AI coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex that guides them toward minimal, non-over-engineered code. Before writing new code, it follows a priority ladder — skip unneeded code (YAGNI), reuse existing code, use the standard library, native platform features, or an installed dependency, or write one line — while never cutting validation, error handling, security, or accessibility.
summary.usage: Installation is host-specific; for Claude Code it requires two separate prompts: `/plugin marketplace add DietrichGebert/ponytail` followed by `/plugin install ponytail@ponytail`. Other hosts, such as Codex and GitHub Copilot CLI, have their own install commands. Slash commands like `/ponytail` and `/ponytail-review` switch between lite, full, ultra, and off intensity levels; a `PONYTAIL_DEFAULT_MODE` environment variable can set the default (full by default).
summary.pros: Benchmarks against a no-skill baseline, run on a real FastAPI + React repo using Claude Code with Haiku 4.5, report ponytail cutting lines of code by 54%, cost by 20%, and time by 27%, while keeping 100% safety — better than a bare 'YAGNI + one-liners' prompt, which dropped to 95% safety.
summary.cons: The Claude Code and Codex plugins rely on two Node.js lifecycle hooks, so `node` must be on PATH or always-on activation stays silent instead of erroring. The headline benchmark numbers come from a small sample (n=4) on one model (Haiku 4.5) and one repo, so the measured gains may not generalize to other codebases or models.
summary.fit: The project reportedly works with 20 agent hosts per its badge, including Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, and OpenCode. The `/ponytail` slash commands need a 'skill-capable host'; instruction-only adapters like Cursor, Windsurf, Cline, Copilot Chat, Kiro, and Antigravity load the always-on ruleset but without the commands.

summary.goal: skills is a collection of Claude Code skills published by HumanLayer (https://humanlayer.dev), distributed for installation into a project.
summary.usage: Skills are installed with `npx skills add humanlayer/skills --skill SKILLNAME`, substituting SKILLNAME with a listed skill name such as improve-claude-md, narrow-react-prop-types, build-iterated-agentic-loop, design-control-loop, or show-me; each is then invoked in the project with its own slash command, for example `/improve-claude-md` or `/show-me`.
summary.pros: The repository offers five distinct skills: tuning CLAUDE.md instruction adherence, narrowing React prop types to live code paths, scaffolding an iterated coding-agent GitHub Actions workflow, interactively designing an agentic control loop, and producing concise explanatory diagrams or HTML artifacts.
summary.cons: Installing skills requires a Node.js environment capable of running `npx skills add humanlayer/skills --skill SKILLNAME`; the README does not describe alternative installation methods or indicate compatibility with non-npm workflows.
summary.fit: This project appears suited for developers already using Claude Code who want ready-made, narrowly scoped skills for documentation tuning, React typing, agentic workflow scaffolding, or visual explanations, rather than a general-purpose standalone tool.

repos.name: openai / plugins
repos.description: OpenAI Plugins

summary.usage: Each plugin is organized under plugins/<name>/ and must include a .codex-plugin/plugin.json manifest, with optional companion files like skills/, .app.json, .mcp.json, agents/, commands/, hooks.json, and assets/. The default marketplace configuration is located at .agents/plugins/marketplace.json, pointing to the plugins/ directory.
summary.pros: The repository offers several richer, real-world examples spanning design (Figma), knowledge work (Notion), mobile/desktop development (build-ios-apps, build-macos-apps, expo), and web deployment (build-web-apps, netlify), giving developers multiple reference implementations for learning plugin structure.
summary.cons: Users authenticating with an API key appear to rely on a separate marketplace file (.agents/plugins/api_marketplace.json) rather than the default one, which suggests the plugin discovery setup may differ depending on login method and could require additional configuration awareness.
summary.fit: This repository appears best suited for developers already working within the Codex ecosystem who want reference examples for building or extending plugins across design, productivity, and app-development domains, rather than for those seeking a single standalone tool.

repos.name: tt-a1i / archify
repos.description: Agent skill for beautiful, verifiable architecture, workflow, sequence, data-flow, and lifecycle diagrams—self-contained HTML with motion and crisp export.

summary.goal: Archify is a Node.js rendering and validation system for AI coding agents (Cursor, Claude Code, Codex CLI, and OpenCode) that turns a codebase or system description into an interactive system map directly in chat. Agents produce typed JSON IR that Archify deterministically compiles into HTML/SVG diagrams.
summary.usage: Install globally with `npx skills add tt-a1i/archify -g`, then describe a system in an agent chat (no repository required) or ask the agent to analyze a repository and generate an architecture diagram. The CLI also offers commands such as `node archify/bin/archify.mjs guide "Show an API request with Redis cache miss"` for choosing a diagram type.
summary.pros: Output passes atomic checks (schema, layout, HTML/SVG, routing) before delivery, and interactions like tracing reach or routes reuse only authored data rather than inventing topology. Results are portable as a single self-contained HTML file, with optional PNG, SVG, WebM, and share-card exports, plus an Architecture Delta mode that compares Before/After snapshots for review.
summary.cons: Archify explicitly excludes automatic Mermaid parsing, general-purpose auto-layout, hosted sharing, and WYSIWYG editing, positioning it as neither a general drawing editor nor a Mermaid theme. Some features, such as the deployment-ownership profile, fail closed and require explicitly authored data (owners, region, database scope) rather than inspecting live infrastructure.
summary.fit: Archify appears suited to developers using supported agent CLIs/IDEs (Cursor, Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, and via ZIP, Claude.ai or Raven) who want agent-generated architecture, workflow, sequence, data-flow, or lifecycle diagrams for documentation or pre-merge review, rather than teams needing a general-purpose interactive diagram editor.

repos.name: mksglu / context-mode
repos.description: Context window optimization for AI coding agents. Sandboxes tool output (98% reduction), persists session memory, and   enforces routing across 17 platforms via MCP + hooks.

summary.goal: Context Mode is an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server built for AI coding agents. Its documented goal is reducing how much raw tool output — such as file reads, web fetches, and command results — enters the model's context window, while also preserving session state such as edited files and pending tasks across conversation compaction.
summary.usage: Claude Code users install it as a plugin with `/plugin marketplace add mksglu/context-mode` followed by `/plugin install context-mode@context-mode`, then restart Claude Code and run the diagnostics command to confirm the install. The documented prerequisite for this plugin path is Claude Code v1.0.33+; other supported clients register the same server as an MCP tool provider instead.
summary.pros: The README states that raw command output is processed inside an isolated sandbox subprocess, so only relevant results reach the conversation, with one documented example of a 315 KB session output reduced to about 5.4 KB — roughly a 98% reduction. It also documents no telemetry and no required account, since session data stays local.
summary.cons: On platforms without hook support, such as the Antigravity IDE and Zed, the README states that routing enforcement depends on a manually copied instruction file rather than automatic interception, and estimates this reaches only about 60% of the context savings achieved with hooks. The Cursor plugin is also documented as still awaiting marketplace review.
summary.fit: Based on the company logos presented as users, Context Mode appears suited to both individual developers and engineering teams working across MCP-compatible AI coding clients — the README documents support for 17 such clients plus an OpenClaw gateway integration. It is released under the Elastic License 2.0, a source-available license disallowing hosted or managed-service offerings.

repos.name: mattpocock / skills
repos.description: Skills for Real Engineers. Straight from my .agents directory.

summary.goal: mattpocock/skills is a collection of agent skills intended for real software engineering work rather than casual "vibe coding." The skills target common failure modes when working with coding agents: misalignment on requirements, overly verbose agent output, non-working code, and growing codebase complexity.
summary.usage: The skills can be installed as a managed Claude Code plugin with `claude plugins install mattpocock-skills` (or `/plugin install mattpocock-skills` inside a session), which updates automatically, or copied as editable files into a project using `npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills`. After installing, run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` once per repository to configure the issue tracker, triage labels, and documentation location.
summary.pros: Skills are described as small, adaptable, and composable, and work with any model. They are split into user-invoked skills (e.g. grill-me, tdd, code-review) and model-invoked skills that the agent can reach for automatically. The set covers practices such as test-driven development, code review, domain modeling, and architecture review.
summary.cons: Users must choose one installation path: installing both the Claude Code plugin and the skills.sh copy results in every skill being duplicated. The skills.sh version places editable files directly in the project, so keeping them current requires manually running `npx skills update`, rather than receiving automatic updates.
summary.fit: This project appears best suited to engineers who already use Claude Code, Codex, or similar coding agents and want structured, adaptable workflows for real applications, in contrast to fully automated planning frameworks like GSD, BMAD, or Spec-Kit, which are described as taking away control from the developer.

repos.name: blader / humanizer
repos.description: Agent skill that removes signs of AI-generated writing from text

summary.goal: Humanizer is a Markdown-based skill that rewrites AI-sounding text so it reads as if written by a person, without changing what the text says. According to the README, it works with any agent that supports skills.
summary.usage: Install it with the Skills CLI using `npx skills add blader/humanizer --global` for a global install, or omit `--global` for a project-only install; the skill responds to `/humanizer`. On Claude Code 2.1.142 or newer, it can instead be installed as a plugin with `/plugin marketplace add blader/humanizer` and `/plugin install humanizer@humanizer`, responding to `/humanizer:humanizer`. Claude Desktop requires a manual install by downloading the repo as a ZIP or copying SKILL.md into the agent's skill folder.
summary.pros: The rewrite process shows its work: an initial draft, a short critique, and a final version. It edits only prose, leaving code, data, frontmatter, and link targets unchanged, and the README states it does not invent facts, asking for missing details instead. It also supports voice matching from a writing sample, and organizes its checks into 25 numbered patterns ordered by strength and frequency.
summary.cons: Several patterns are documented as 'weak alone,' meaning they justify an edit only when multiple tells appear together in a passage, since a careful writer may use any one deliberately; this suggests some rewrite decisions may need human judgment in ambiguous cases.
summary.fit: This tool appears suited to users of skill-supporting agents such as Claude Code or Claude Desktop who want a documented, pattern-based way to reduce AI-sounding phrasing while preserving factual content; the README does not indicate support for agents lacking skills capability.

repos.name: openai / skills
repos.description: Skills Catalog for Codex

summary.goal: This repository catalogs Agent Skills — folders of instructions, scripts, and resources — for use and distribution with the Codex AI agent platform. Skills package capabilities so teams and individuals can complete tasks in a repeatable way.
summary.usage: Skills in the `.system` folder install automatically in the latest Codex. Curated or experimental skills are installed via the `$skill-installer` command inside Codex, e.g. `$skill-installer gh-address-comments`, or by specifying a GitHub directory URL: `$skill-installer install https://github.com/openai/skills/tree/main/skills/.experimental/create-plan`. Codex must be restarted afterward for the skill to take effect.
summary.pros: Skills are reusable across projects ('write once, use everywhere') and installable with simple named commands through `$skill-installer`. System skills need no manual setup, and the Agent Skills format follows an open standard rather than a proprietary one.
summary.cons: The repository is explicitly marked deprecated, with current Codex skill and plugin examples redirected to the openai/plugins repository, so future updates or support for skills here appear uncertain. A Codex restart is also required after each install.
summary.fit: This repository likely suits existing Codex users wanting prepackaged, repeatable skills, though given the deprecation notice, those seeking current examples would probably be better served by openai/plugins instead. Licensing is defined per skill in its own LICENSE.txt file.

repos.name: heygen-com / hyperframes
repos.description: Write HTML. Render video. Built for agents.

summary.goal: HyperFrames is an open-source (Apache 2.0) framework for turning HTML, CSS, media, and seekable animations into deterministic MP4 videos, usable locally through a CLI, through AI coding agent skills, or as the rendering core behind hosted authoring workflows.
summary.usage: Agents typically install the core skill set with `npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes`, while manual use starts a project with `npx hyperframes init my-video`, then previews and renders it with `npx hyperframes preview` and `npx hyperframes render` to produce an MP4 locally.
summary.pros: HyperFrames compositions are authored as plain HTML with data attributes rather than React, rendering is deterministic so identical input yields the same output, the CLI is non-interactive by default for agent workflows, and the project ships 20 packaged skills plus a components catalog covering common needs like captions, charts, and transitions.
summary.cons: Running HyperFrames locally requires Node.js 22+ and FFmpeg as prerequisites, and cloning the full repository for development additionally requires Git LFS, since the golden regression-test baselines add roughly 240 MB of .mp4 files that must be fetched separately.
summary.fit: Based on its HTML-first, agent-friendly design and deterministic rendering, HyperFrames seems best suited to developers and AI agents automating CI or pipeline video generation, whereas teams already committed to Remotion's React-based authoring model may find switching authoring paradigms less straightforward.

repos.name: cathrynlavery / diagram-design
repos.description: 38 editorial diagram types for Claude Code, Codex, and Pi. Self-contained HTML + SVG. No shadows. No Mermaid slop.

summary.goal: Diagram Design is an Agent Skill that generates 39 editorial-style diagram types (architecture, flowcharts, sequence diagrams, and more) as self-contained HTML and SVG for Claude Code, Codex, Factory Droid, Pi, and other Agent Skills-compatible hosts. It appears to target developers and writers who want on-brand, non-generic diagrams without relying on Figma or default AI-generated styling.
summary.usage: Install via `/plugin marketplace add cathrynlavery/diagram-design` followed by `/plugin install diagram-design@diagram-design` in Claude Code (similar commands exist for Codex, GitHub Copilot, Factory Droid, and Pi). After installing, users can open `skills/diagram-design/assets/index.html` to browse all 39 diagrams, or ask the agent in natural language to produce a specific diagram type.
summary.pros: Diagrams ship as a single self-contained HTML file with no build step, JavaScript, or external image dependency. Accessibility is built in by default (ARIA roles, resolving accessible names, WCAG AA contrast checks), and the skill can also redraw existing draw.io, Mermaid, or Excalidraw sources while producing a fidelity ledger of what changed.
summary.cons: PNG export requires a one-time separate setup step (`pip install playwright && playwright install chromium`), which adds an external dependency beyond the core skill install. Auto-update for third-party marketplaces is also disabled by default in Claude Code, requiring a manual toggle to keep the plugin current.
summary.fit: Documented use cases where this skill is not recommended include quick unicode diagrams for tweets or terminals, plain lists, before/after comparisons, and single-box diagrams, suggesting it fits multi-node, structured diagrams rather than simple content. It seems best suited for teams that want diagrams matching their website's brand colors and fonts through the onboarding flow.

repos.name: fmtlib / fmt
repos.description: A modern formatting library

summary.goal: {fmt} is an open-source C++ formatting library described in its README as a fast and safe alternative to C stdio and C++ iostreams, implementing the C++20 std::format and C++23 std::print interfaces.
summary.usage: It is used by including a header such as `#include <fmt/core.h>` and calling functions like `fmt::print("Hello, world!\n");` to format and print text; documentation is hosted at https://fmt.dev.
summary.pros: The README reports fmt can be tens of percent to 20–30 times faster than sprintf and iostreams for numeric formatting, with a single-threaded file-writing example cited as up to 9 times faster than fprintf; it also uses the Dragonbox algorithm for IEEE 754 floating-point formatting with correct rounding, offers compile-time format-string checking, and ships under a permissive MIT license with no external dependencies.
summary.cons: Benchmark figures in the README, measured on one specific machine (an Apple M5 Max running macOS 26.6.2 with Apple Clang 21.0.0), show optimized-build compile times of about 5.1 seconds for fmt 12.2 headers versus 1.6 seconds for plain printf and 49.1 seconds for Boost Format 1.92, so fmt adds measurable compile-time overhead compared to printf, though results may differ on other compilers or platforms.
summary.fit: Based on the notable adopters it lists, including ClickHouse, MongoDB, PyTorch, and Windows Terminal, fmt appears best suited to C++ projects that need high-performance, type-safe text formatting, though its fit for minimal-footprint or embedded contexts is not directly addressed.

repos.name: coreyhaines31 / marketingskills

Moving an existing product marketing context file to its new location and filename is also a manual step, though old paths reportedly still work as a fallback.

repos.name: ChromeDevTools / chrome-devtools-mcp
repos.description: Chrome DevTools for coding agents

summary.usage: An MCP client is configured to run `npx -y chrome-devtools-mcp@latest` to start the chrome-devtools-mcp server; for basic browser tasks only, the `--slim` and `--headless` flags can be added. A first test prompt asking to check the performance of a URL confirms the browser opens and records a trace.

summary.fit: chrome-devtools-mcp appears suited for developers building agentic tooling who want an integrated browser subagent for automation, debugging, and performance analysis, though by default it collects usage statistics and can send trace URLs to Google's CrUX API unless disabled with flags.

repos.name: microsoft / markitdown
repos.description: Python tool for converting files and office documents to Markdown.

summary.goal: MarkItDown is a lightweight Python utility, documented as most comparable to textract, for converting files such as PDF, PowerPoint, Word, Excel, images, audio, HTML, and other formats to Markdown for use with LLMs and related text analysis pipelines.
summary.usage: Requiring Python 3.10 or higher, MarkItDown is installed with `pip install 'markitdown[all]'` and run from the command line as `markitdown path-to-file.pdf > document.md`; the README also documents an equivalent Python API using `from markitdown import MarkItDown` and `md.convert(...)`.
summary.pros: The README states MarkItDown preserves document structure such as headings, lists, tables, and links as Markdown, describes Markdown as token-efficient for LLMs, and documents optional per-format dependency groups plus a third-party plugin system for extending supported formats.
summary.cons: MarkItDown performs I/O with the privileges of the current process and the README instructs sanitizing untrusted inputs before conversion; it also notes the Markdown output may not be the best option for high-fidelity document conversions intended for human consumption.
summary.fit: The README frames MarkItDown as a Python library meant to be incorporated into other systems, suggesting it is not intended for direct deployment as a standalone application, since its contribution scope explicitly excludes web servers, REST APIs, and desktop or browser-based interfaces.

repos.name: ruvnet / ruflo
repos.description: 🌊 The original agent harness. Deploy intelligent multi-player swarms, coordinate autonomous workflows, and build conversational AI systems. repos.name: THU-MAIC / OpenMAIC
repos.description: Open Multi-Agent Interactive Classroom — Get an immersive, multi-agent learning experience in just one click

summary.goal: OpenMAIC (Open Multi-Agent Interactive Classroom) is an open-source AI platform that turns a topic or document into an interactive classroom, generating slides, quizzes, simulations, and project-based learning activities delivered by AI teachers and classmates. Copy `.env.example` to `.env.local` and set at least one LLM provider API key. Start it with `pnpm dev` and open http://localhost:3000. Node.js >= 22.19 and pnpm >= 10 are required; Docker and Vercel deployment are also documented.

Lessons export as editable .pptx or self-contained HTML, and offline exports inline external assets for air-gapped playback. The interface supports 12 locales, and an OpenMAIC Skill lets it be triggered from agent workbenches like OpenClaw, Codex, DeepSeek, or WorkBuddy.

summary.fit: Based on its use-case examples — generating lessons on programming, game rules, or research papers — OpenMAIC seems best suited to individual learners, educators, and developers wanting to self-host or extend an AI-driven course-authoring platform, rather than users seeking a fully managed, zero-configuration service.

repos.name: Tencent / WeKnora
repos.description: Open-source LLM knowledge platform: turn raw documents into a queryable RAG, an autonomous reasoning agent, and a self-maintaining Wiki.

It combines RAG-based Quick Q&A, a ReAct Agent that orchestrates retrieval and tools, and a Wiki Mode that turns raw documents into an interlinked, self-maintaining markdown knowledge base.
summary.usage: Set up by running `git clone https://github.com/Tencent/WeKnora.git`, then `cd WeKnora` and `docker compose up -d` to start core services (Docker, Docker Compose, and Git are listed prerequisites). It is released under the MIT License and describes a fully modular, self-hostable architecture where LLMs, vector stores, and storage can be swapped.

summary.fit: Given its stated emphasis on local or private-cloud deployment and full data sovereignty, WeKnora seems best suited for organizations seeking a self-hosted, enterprise document Q&A and knowledge-base platform rather than a ready-made managed cloud service.

repos.name: jakubkrehel / skills
repos.description: A collection of agent skills that help you build a great interface.

The skills reflect topics the author covers on their personal website and the Interfaces design engineering publication.

repos.name: every-app / open-seo
repos.description: Open source alternative to Semrush and Ahrefs

Plans to simplify hosting on platforms like Railway, Coolify, or Dokploy in coming months suggest current support for those platforms may be more limited.
summary.fit: OpenSEO appears suited to individuals or small teams wanting SEO workflows such as keyword research, rank tracking, competitor insights, backlinks, site audits, and AI visibility, combined with AI-agent integration. The free trial and Docker path seem suited to personal evaluation, while Cloudflare, usable on a free plan, appears intended for team, internet-facing use.

repos.name: omacom / omarchy
repos.description: Beautiful, Modern & Opinionated Linux

repos.name: anthropics / claude-plugins-community
repos.description: Community plugin marketplace for Claude Cowork and Claude Code. Read-only mirror — submit plugins at clau.de/plugin-directory-submission.

repos.name: cordiverse / cordis
repos.description: Meta-Framework of Spatiotemporal Composability
